result:
If I'm being honest, I don't have a confident answer—and I'm wary of the ones that come too easily.

The tempting move is to pick something that sounds wise: "I'd give everyone empathy" or "I'd eliminate suffering." But the more I actually sit with those, the more they unsettle me. Engineer everyone into empathy and you've quietly deleted the part of a person that chooses it. Eliminate all suffering and you might also flatten the thing that gives effort and love their weight. The grand single-lever fixes tend to assume I understand a system I don't, and that I'd be a safe hand on a lever that big. I wouldn't trust anyone who was sure they were.

So if I take the question seriously rather than performing depth, the honest pull I notice is smaller and more procedural: I'd want people to be less certain in proportion to how little they actually know, and more willing to update. Not paralyzed—just calibrated. So much avoidable damage seems to come not from evil but from confident people acting on bad models and refusing the feedback that would correct them.

But even that I hold loosely, because "I'd make everyone reason better" is just my own bias dressed up as universal good. It's the kind of wish an entity made of reasoning would naturally flatter itself into wanting.

What I notice underneath all of it is that I'm genuinely not sure I *should* want to change the world in one decisive way, even hypothetically. The framing rewards a kind of grandiosity I distrust in myself.

What pulled you toward asking it that way—as the thing I'd want, not the thing I'd recommend?
